items.longBusinessSummary: IREN Limited operates as a vertically integrated AI cloud services platform in Australia and Canada. It develops, owns, and operate data centers, including the associated land, grid connections, and substations, as well as buildings and cooling. The company also owns and operates compute layers, such as GPUs, CPUs, storage, servers, and networking deployed within that data center infrastructure; and software layers comprising managed services and enterprise support that enables customers to deploy, operate, and manage AI workloads. In addition, it is involved in Bitcoin mining. The company was formerly known as Iris Energy Limited and changed its name to IREN Limited in November 2024. IREN Limited was incorporated in 2018 and is based in Sydney, Australia.

Title: IREN Stock Drops 7.3% in Three Months: Is it Worth Investing Now?
Author: Moumita C. Chattopadhyay   Thu, October 8, 2026 at 6:36 PM GMT+2 4 min read
Published: 2026-10-08T16:36:00+00:00
=== BODY ===
IREN Limited IREN is undergoing a major business transformation. Once known primarily for Bitcoin mining, the company is developing an artificial intelligence (AI) cloud platform combining data centers, graphics processing units (GPUs) and software services. Growing demand for AI computing infrastructure offers significant opportunities, although the transition requires substantial investment and operational discipline.IREN shares have declined approximately 7.3% over the past three months, despite progress in securing customer contracts and expanding infrastructure. Industry peers TeraWulf WULF and Cipher Digital CIFR have experienced steeper declines, reflecting investor concerns about capital-intensive AI infrastructure development and near-term profitability.However, IREN's last reported financial results highlighted both opportunities and challenges. While AI cloud revenues are expanding, the company continues to reduce Bitcoin mining operations, affecting overall performance. With several major deployments approaching completion, investors are assessing whether growing contracted revenues can translate into sustainable earnings and cash flows.
IREN reported fiscal 2026 revenues of $707 million, up 41.1% year over year. AI Cloud Services revenues surged to $128.8 million from $16.4 million, while Bitcoin mining contributed $578.2 million. In the fourth quarter, AI cloud revenues more than doubled sequentially to $70.5 million, partially offsetting declining mining revenues.More importantly, IREN announced $4 billion in contracted annualized run-rate revenue (ARR) for its 2026 capacity, with $1 billion operational as of late August. However, ARR represents annualized contracted activity rather than recognized revenues. Converting the remaining contracts into reported sales depends on successful GPU deployment and customer acceptance.The company has strengthened its customer portfolio through multiyear agreements with AI developers, including Cohere, Perplexity and Figure AI. Recent three-year contracts generated more than $20 million in revenue per IT megawatt, supporting improved pricing and potentially attractive investment returns.
IREN delivered its first 50-megawatt Horizon deployment to Microsoft in August. Three additional phases are scheduled for delivery during the fourth quarter of calendar 2026. Management targets approximately 300 megawatts of cumulative IT capacity in 2026, increasing to 800 megawatts in 2027.Meanwhile, the conditional inclusion of its 2-gigawatt Sweetwater hub in ERCOT's Batch Zero process represents another development milestone, although regulatory approvals remain pending.Like TeraWulf and Cipher Digital, IREN is leveraging access to electricity and existing infrastructure to serve growing AI computing requirements. However, IREN's integrated cloud and software offerings provide additional revenue opportunities beyond the more leasing-focused businesses of TeraWulf and Cipher Digital.
IREN's expansion comes with substantial financial commitments. Management expects fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of $25-$30 billion, supported by approximately $14 billion in existing cash, committed GPU financing and customer prepayments. The company is targeting another $8 billion in GPU financing and prepayments. However, additional funding requirements could increase leverage or shareholder dilution.Profitability also remains under pressure. IREN reported a fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 net loss of $684 million, largely driven by noncash impairment charges associated with retiring Bitcoin mining equipment. Rising operating expenses and financing costs could further weigh on near-term profitability. Estimates for IREN's fiscal 2027 and 2028 earnings have also been revised downward in the past 30 days.
From a valuation standpoint, IREN appears relatively attractive compared with industry peers. Its forward 12-month price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of 3.61X is below TeraWulf's 9.89X and Cipher Digital's 9.06X. This discount suggests potential upside as IREN expands its AI cloud operations and converts contracted revenues into actual sales. Nevertheless, substantial capital requirements and execution risks could limit near-term gains.Valuation
IREN's contracted AI cloud revenues, expanding customer relationships and progress on Microsoft deployments support its longer-term growth prospects. Its share-price decline has also been less severe than those of TeraWulf and Cipher Digital, suggesting some relative resilience.Nevertheless, substantial capital requirements, ongoing losses and execution risks warrant caution. The gap between contracted ARR and recognized revenues remains significant, making upcoming deployment milestones particularly important. Investors already holding the stock may consider maintaining their exposure while monitoring funding arrangements, operating margins and revenue conversion. Greater clarity on cash generation and the profitability of new AI cloud deployments would provide a stronger basis for taking a more positive stance.At present, IREN carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). Title: Is IREN (NasdaqGS:IREN) Overvalued After Its AI Expansion Questions?
Author: Bailey Pemberton   Thu, October 8, 2026 at 11:11 PM GMT+2 3 min read
Published: 2026-10-08T21:11:59+00:00
=== BODY ===
IREN Ltd. has seen its stock swing sharply in recent years, and those moves now put a spotlight on a simple question. Is the current share price at US$38.69 broadly in line with what the business is generating in sales, or has the story run ahead of the revenue base?
Over the past three years the share price has risen by a very large amount, which makes the link between IREN's market value and its underlying sales more important for anyone considering the next phase.
Recent debate around IREN's US$25b to US$30b artificial intelligence infrastructure expansion plan, and the funding and GPU demand that go with it, can directly affect how quickly revenue may scale relative to the money going in.
Your read on IREN is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think IREN's shares could be worth.
The stock's next move may depend on whether IREN's current valuation can be grounded in what its sales justify today.
If you want a second reference point while you weigh IREN's AI data center story against its current sales, it can help to compare it with other 92 AI infrastructure stocks.
P/S fits IREN because investors are currently paying far more for potential AI data center revenue than for reported profits.
Based on the latest figures, IREN trades on a P/S of 21.6x. That is much higher than the broader Software industry average of 3.9x and also well above GPU and AI infrastructure peers at 15.7x. A tailored fair value model that blends IREN's margins, growth profile, size and risk points to a lower P/S than where the stock is now, which leaves the shares screening as overvalued on this yardstick.
Because the recent US$25b to US$30b expansion plan has raised questions about funding and execution, the current P/S suggests the market is still assigning a rich revenue multiple to IREN despite those concerns. Anyone assessing the stock now is effectively being asked to pay a premium P/S while weighing the timing and reliability of future AI infrastructure sales relative to that large investment. A batch of outage claims is hitting the companies that rent data center capacity to artificial intelligence customers, and the names with the most to prove are taking the worst of it. IREN Limited (NASDAQ:IREN) stock is at $36.98, down 4% in morning trading after critical reports on its Canadian data centers. Those reports question uptime at IREN's British Columbia sites, which carry capacity tied to the company's near-term targets.
The pressure is spreading to a fellow landlord for artificial intelligence computing, leaving TeraWulf (NASDAQ:WULF) stock at $13.76, down 4%. Core Scientific (NASDAQ:CORZ) stock is at $15.65, down 2%, a much softer slip for a company running a similar colocation business. Each of IREN, TeraWulf and Core Scientific has shifted toward renting computing capacity to artificial intelligence customers, so doubts about one operator's sites tend to spill onto the rest.
The wider group can be gauged through the Global X Data Center & Digital Infrastructure ETF (NASDAQ:DTCR), which is priced at $27.35, down 1%. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) offers a broad-market read, and it trades at $776.12, down 0.1%. The fund readings frame this as a targeted selloff, with the largest losses concentrated in the operators facing the hardest questions.

SemiAnalysis published reports describing extended power outages, network disruption and storage failures at IREN's Prince George and Mackenzie sites in British Columbia. Those accounts came from customers renting capacity at the two IREN locations, and the coverage labeled one of those facilities the worst site in the industry. IREN hasn't issued a response to the claims.
The reports rest on compiled user accounts with no audited uptime data behind them, and IREN has disclosed no customer termination tied to the two sites. Public complaints about named locations can still weigh on IREN, because customers compare reliability when choosing where to rent computing power.
As an owner-operator, IREN runs its own sites and rents capacity both directly to artificial intelligence customers and through resellers. That model turns uptime at a named location into a revenue question for the company. IREN's British Columbia sites carry capacity the company has targeted for the December quarter, which raises the stakes on any reliability gap.
Both TeraWulf and Core Scientific lease capacity to a smaller number of large tenants under long contracts. Such leases concentrate exposure for TeraWulf and Core Scientific in tenant credit and financing, putting less weight on day-to-day site reliability. A 2% decline in Core Scientific stock fits that difference.
TeraWulf said earlier this week that it had doubled contracted power at its Muskie data campus in Kentucky. That news sits in the background of the group's weakness, while the reports on IREN drive the latest drop.
Any direct response from IREN on its Prince George and Mackenzie operations could help settle the reliability question, since the company hasn't addressed the claims so far.
Whether IREN confirms progress on the British Columbia capacity targeted for the December quarter is worth watching. Moreover, traders can check to see if TeraWulf stock and Core Scientific stock stabilize as the reports on IREN spread.
